s.en: Mornings in the steam city of Vern begin with the sound of whistles.
When the factories of the lower ring all belch out their smoke at once, the sky turns grey in an instant.
Even so, there is one thing you can see from anywhere in the city.
The Great Clock Tower, soaring at the city's heart.
Its white dial, jutting up above the smoke, is said to have kept time for over a hundred years without drifting a single second.
Sera Milford loved gazing at that dial from her little attic window.
"...Three more minutes."
The instant she burrowed back under the blanket, a bellow came flying up from downstairs.
"Sera! How long are you gonna lie there? Time to open the shop."
"I'm up, I'm up, I said!"
Her grandfather Oz has run a clock shop here in the lower ring for forty years.
His hands are sure; his mouth is foul.
Sera slipped into her uniform, tied her hair back in one, and ran down the creaking stairs.
In the shop front on the ground floor, broken clocks stand in rows.
Cuckoo clocks, mantel clocks, sturdy pocket watches of the kind train drivers use.
Every one of them seemed to be waiting for the day it would go home to its owner.
Among them is a single clock that isn't for sale.
A silver pocket watch, set at the corner of the workbench.
On its lid is engraved a crest she has never seen anywhere, and its hands, pointing at 3:17, never so much as twitch.
It has been that way ever since the day, ten years ago, when her mother disappeared.
Every morning, Sera begins her day by opening this watch.
She checks the gears one by one, oils them, winds the mainspring.
There is nothing broken anywhere.
And yet, this one watch never moved.
"Morning, Mom. No luck today either, huh."
Murmuring softly, she closed the lid and tucked the watch into the breast pocket of her uniform.
She does it every day. It's a sort of good-luck charm.
"Your mother's watch again?"
Oz appeared from the back of the shop carrying two steaming mugs.
Deep in his white beard, his mouth is bent into a scowl.
"What won't be fixed won't be fixed. Waste of time."
"Is that a thing a craftsman should say?"
"Besides, whether it's a waste is for me to decide."
Oz snorted, but said nothing more.
Instead, he sets one of the mugs down in front of her.
Inside: the usual substitute coffee, bitter and faintly sweet.
"Isn't today the Academy's tour day? Drink up and get going."
"That's right! Today we get to go inside the Great Clock Tower!"
"It's a once-a-year tour — I can't be late!"
Sera downed her coffee in one gulp, grabbed her bag and ran for the door.
Just then, she thought she felt the pocket watch in her breast pocket make a faint sound.
But when she took it out to look, its hands still pointed at 3:17, motionless as ever.
The only way up from the lower ring to the upper is the steam lift.
Among the workers crammed into the iron cage, Sera made herself small.
Down here, the Academy's navy uniform can't help standing out.
"Yo, Sera! Gloomy face first thing in the morning, huh."
Pushing through the tide of people, a lanky, tall boy stuck his head out.
Niko, from the same Mechanics course.
Eldest of six, born into a canal boatman's family, he has never managed to shake the merchant quarter's dialect.
"My face is how I was born. What about you — what happened to those oily hands?"
"These? Spent all last night tinkering with my flying machine's engine."
"It's this close to actually flying, I swear."
"You said that last time too, and fell off the warehouse roof."
"I didn't fall. I just botched the landing."

t: ずにはいられなかった
s.en: He said it with such a serious face that Sera couldn't help laughing.
Talking with Niko, her morning gloom always flies off somewhere.
The lift lurched with a clunk; overhead, the thick chains groaned.
The moment they pass through the layer of smoke, the window floods with light.
Blue sky. White stone streets.
And, looming right in front of her, the enormous dial of the Great Clock Tower.
She saw it every day, and yet today, too, Sera caught her breath without meaning to.
Step off the lift, and you are in another world.
Horseless steam carriages glide quietly down the cobbled avenue.
At the fountain in the square, a chronomancer is stopping the falling water in midair to delight the children.
In the upper ring, chronomancy is simply part of everyday life.
But only those born with a sigil somewhere on their bodies can use it.
On Sera's body, search where you like, there isn't one.
That's why she's in Mechanics, not Chronomancy.
The department that achieves with gears and steam what chronomancy can't — it sounds nice put that way, but at the Academy it went by "the oil-stinking dropouts' club."
Passing through the main gate of the Royal Vern Academy, they found a crowd gathered in the courtyard.
At the centre of the ring stood a girl with her silver hair pinned up high.
Gleaming at her breast: two crossed clock hands — the crest of House Eisen.
Top of the first-year Chronomancy class: Viola Eisen.
"Ugh, Her Ladyship. Got a whole flock of hangers-on with her again today."
"Don't look. It's a pain if you meet her eyes."
But it was too late.
Viola's violet eyes locked straight onto Sera.
"Oh my. I wondered why the morning smelled of oil — it's the Mechanics people."
Her circle of students tittered.
"Today's tour of the Great Clock Tower is a special event for the Chronomancy course."
"I do wonder why the gear-fiddlers are tagging along."
Sera clenched her fists.
If it was comebacks she wanted, she had mountains of them.
But someone attending on a scholarship can't afford to pick a fight with the daughter of a great house.
— or so she'd thought, but her mouth was already moving on its own.
"Half of what keeps the Great Clock Tower running is mechanical engineering."
"So I'd say we've got plenty of reason to tour it."
The courtyard fell dead silent.
Viola raised a fan to her lips and looked Sera over, head to toe.
"...And your name is?"
"Sera. Sera Milford."
"Miss Milford. I shall remember that."
With only that, Viola turned on her heel.
Only — just before she left, for the briefest instant, those violet eyes went to the tools peeking out of Sera's bag.
With eyes like someone looking at a rare jewel.
"...You really don't know the meaning of fear, do you."
"I said it... What do I do, Niko?"
"Can't be helped. I'll gather up your bones."
The inside of the Great Clock Tower was the belly of a gigantic machine.
However far up you looked, gears overlapped upon gears, layer after layer.
The small ones were the size of a palm, the big ones as large as a house, and they turned in perfect rhythm, as if all playing a single piece of music.
It smelled of oil and iron and, faintly, of thunder.
Sera begrudged herself even a blink.
"Everyone, please watch your step."
It was Instructor Regen, in charge of the Mechanics course, speaking in his quiet voice.
A thin, greying man with permanently sleepy eyes — and yet not a single student had ever dozed off in his class.
"What you see at the tower's core is the time crystal."
"Every act of chronomancy and every steam engine in Vern draws its power from that crystal."
There it was, where the teacher pointed.
In the middle of the forest of gears, an enormous crystal giving off blue light was slowly pulsing.
Like the heart of the tower itself.
Even the Chronomancy students were gaping up at it, mouths open.
Only Viola, by a railing a little apart from the rest, was staring at the crystal with a hard expression.
"...Just as I feared. The light is weakening."
Sera was probably the only one who heard that small murmur.
It happened in the very next instant.
Deep inside the tower, something came loose with a clank.
The crystal's light went out, just like that.
And then — every sound vanished.
The turning gears stopped dead.
Dust that had swirled up hung in midair, unmoving.
Students and teacher alike stood frozen, like figures in a painting.
Time has stopped — Sera had that thought for only the briefest instant.
With a boom she felt in her gut, the world lurched into motion again.
With the jolt, one of the gears overhead came off its axle.
A mass of iron as big as a house slowly began to tip.
Directly beneath it was Viola.
"Look out!"
Sera shouted and broke into a run.
But it was too far. She wouldn't make it.
Viola looks up. Her violet eyes, reflecting the falling shadow, fly wide open.
Just then, something in Sera's breast pocket trembled, hot.
Her mother's pocket watch.
Click — a tiny sound.
A sound she had not heard once in ten years — the sound of the hands moving.
The next instant, the hands began to turn backwards.
The tipping gear slid smoothly back to where it had been.
Her running feet carried her backwards of their own accord.
The students' screams were sucked back into their mouths.
Like a music box wound the wrong way, the world unravelled and rewound.
When she came to herself, Sera was standing by the railing.
The crystal was glowing blue.
The gears were turning as if nothing had happened.
A little way off, Viola was staring at the crystal — in exactly the pose she had held before, to the hair.
"...Just as I feared. The light is weakening."
The same words. The same voice.
It wasn't a dream. Time had gone back.
There was no time to think.
Sera kicked off from the floor.
Deep in the tower: clank. The crystal's light goes out, and every sound stops.
And then — boom — the world starts moving again.
By the time the gear overhead came off its axle, Sera was already right in front of Viola.
"Sorry!"
She all but tackled Viola, wrapped her in her arms, and rolled across the floor.
A moment later the giant gear slammed down where the two of them had been, and the whole tower shook like an earthquake.
The iron railing had crumpled like paper craft.
In the billowing dust, Sera coughed.
Viola, in her arms, was staring wide-eyed at the crumpled railing.
"Just now — you had started running before the gear fell, hadn't you."
"As if you had known from the start that it would fall."
Sera couldn't answer.
She didn't know herself what had happened.
When she put a hand to her breast pocket, the watch was still faintly warm.
Gently, she opened the lid.
The hands no longer pointed at 3:17.
The thin second hand was ticking away, slowly — backwards.
"...Mom. What is this?"
All around them, students were crying and shouting.
Somewhere far off, she could hear Instructor Regen barking out orders.
Viola rose unsteadily and, without so much as touching her tousled hair, stared intently at the watch in Sera's hand.
"That watch... where did you come by it?"
"It's my mother's... keepsake, sort of. But why?"
"No. Never mind — not now."
Viola started to say something, then closed her mouth.
Then she brushed the dust from her skirt with awkward hands and, still looking away, added in a small voice:
"...For having been rescued, you have my thanks, Miss Milford."
Red to the tips of her ears as she said it, Viola walked briskly away.
Viola Eisen — that Viola Eisen — had said thank you.

s.en: Sera could do nothing but stare blankly after her.
"Sera! You okay?! What was that just now — when did you even get over there?"
"...I don't know either."
That was the truth.
But one thing was certain.
In that moment, time really had rewound.
By the power of this watch, which had not moved once in ten years.
At around the same time.
At the very top of the Great Clock Tower, from behind its enormous dial, a man was looking down.
A grey greatcoat. A grey mask.
Behind the mask, his eyes narrowed in a smile.
"She answered the crystal's stopping with a rewind, did she."
"Ten years I have searched. This time, I cannot let her slip away."
In the man's hand, a silver pocket watch was quietly ticking.
On its lid was engraved the very same crest as on Sera's.
The only difference was that its hands were turning — the right way round.
